lead: At 1 kHz a transistor's internal capacitors are open circuits, so gain is flat. At 1 MHz they shunt the signal and gain falls. The capacitor from output back to input, Cμ, is the worst: its ends move oppositely, so it draws much more current than its size suggests. This is the Miller effect. It sets the upper cut-off frequency fH, where gain drops to 0.707 of midband.
prereq: You need the hybrid-pi model, rπ and gm from Unit 2, Transistor Biasing and Small-Signal Amplifiers, plus midband gain and RC time constants from Chapter 3.1.

blocks.text: The hybrid-pi model of Unit 2 is a midband model. It keeps rπ and gm and discards every capacitor inside the transistor. That works while each capacitor has reactance far larger than nearby resistors. At higher frequency the reactance falls and these capacitors shunt the signal.

items: Cπ, base to emitter. Typical 10 pF to 200 pF; grows with DC collector current. It is mostly charge stored in the base by the forward-biased emitter junction.
Cμ, base to collector. Typical 1 pF to 10 pF; shrinks as collector-base voltage rises. It is mostly depletion charge of the reverse-biased collector-base junction.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call Cπ diffusion capacitance and Cμ transition capacitance. The model still has only two capacitors.

rπ is base-emitter resistance in ohms: rπ = V_T/I_B, where V_T ≈ 26 mV at room temperature and I_B is DC base current. gm is transconductance in siemens: gm = I_C/V_T, where I_C is DC collector current. Also gm rπ = β, where β is DC current gain.

The FET model has the same shape but no rπ. At low frequency its insulated gate draws no current. Its capacitors are Cgs, gate to source, and Cgd, gate to drain, both a few pF. Above midband these two dominate.

Current through a capacitor C is jωC times the voltage across it, where ω = 2πf is angular frequency in rad/s. Connect C between input and output of an inverting amplifier with gain −A, where A > 0 is gain magnitude. The output moves opposite to the input, so the capacitor voltage exceeds the input voltage.

items: Input node is V_in; output node is V_out = −A V_in.
Voltage across Cμ = V_in − V_out = V_in(1 + A).
Current from input node through Cμ = jωCμ V_in(1 + A).
A capacitor C_eq to ground would draw jωC_eq V_in.

blocks.text: C_eq is the Miller capacitance. Nothing was added; the input node behaves as if a much larger capacitor sat on it.

blocks.where: C_M is Miller input capacitance in farads; Cμ is physical collector-base or gate-drain capacitance in farads; |A_v| is midband voltage gain magnitude between those nodes, dimensionless.

blocks.text: The same capacitor loads the output less: seen from output, the Miller output capacitance is C_out ≈ Cμ(1 + 1/|A_v|) ≈ Cμ. For A = 100 the factor is 1.01.

blocks.where: C_out is extra capacitance at the output node in farads; other symbols are as above. For |A_v| ≥ 10 this is within 10 % of Cμ.

blocks.text: Use (1 + |A_v|), never |A_v| alone. At A = 100 they differ by 1 %; at A = 4 they differ by 20 %. A FET obeys C_M = Cgd(1 + |A_v|); Cgd of 1–5 pF with gain 50 becomes 50–250 pF. Miller multiplication applies to any impedance between input and output: a resistor there is divided by (1 + A).

sections.h3: Upper cut-off frequency and why the CE stage is slow

items: Replace source and bias resistors by one input resistance: R_eq = R_s ‖ R_B ‖ rπ, in ohms, where R_s is source resistance, R_B is bias network seen from base, rπ is base-emitter resistance.
Add input capacitances: C_eq = Cπ + C_M, in farads.
Input time constant: τ_in = R_eq C_eq, in seconds.
Input pole: f_in = 1/(2π R_eq C_eq), in hertz.
At output: R_out = R_C ‖ R_L ‖ r_o and C_out' = Cμ(1 + 1/|A_v|), giving f_out = 1/(2π R_out C_out'). R_C is collector resistor, R_L load, r_o transistor output resistance.
fH is the lower of f_in and f_out, because the lower pole bends gain down first.

blocks.where: fH is upper cut-off frequency in hertz, where |A_v| falls to 0.707 of midband (3 dB down); R_eq is input-node resistance in ohms; C_eq = Cπ + Cμ(1 + |A_v|) is input-node capacitance in farads.

blocks.text: The lower pole is the dominant pole, and fH ≈ f_dominant. Two close poles pull gain down slightly earlier; the estimate is standard and good when poles are far apart.

A CE stage is slow because Cμ is multiplied by full gain while rπ is only a few kΩ. Hundreds of pF times a few kΩ gives microseconds, so fH is tens of kHz. A CB stage escapes: input is emitter and base is grounded, so Cμ runs from collector to ground and sees no gain multiplication. A CS stage has the CE problem exactly, with Cgd replacing Cμ.

The standard cure is the cascode from Unit 2. A common-base transistor sits above the input device and holds its collector almost still, so gain across its own Cμ is near 1 and Miller multiplication almost vanishes. Chapter 3.4 builds on this.

figure.caption: Cπ loads the input by 10 pF, but feedback capacitor Cμ of 2 pF appears as 202 pF Miller capacitance because stage gain is −100. The dashed path is the physical capacitor; the input node feels the large one.

spec.aria: The feedback capacitor Cμ from output to input appears at the input node as a 202 pF Miller capacitance, shunting the input alongside the 10 pF Cπ of the transistor.

examples.question: A CE stage has |A_v| = 100, Cμ = 2 pF, Cπ = 10 pF, R_s = 1 kΩ. Bias network and rπ are large enough to ignore. Find (a) Miller input capacitance, (b) total input capacitance, (c) upper cut-off set by input pole, (d) Miller output capacitance.
steps: C_eq = Cπ + C_M = 10 pF + 202 pF = 212 pF. Cπ is added once because it goes to ground.
examples.answer: C_M = 202 pF, total input capacitance 212 pF, C_out = 2.02 pF, and fH ≈ 751 kHz.
examples.check:
import math
Rs = 1000.0
Av = 100.0
Cmu = 2e-12
Cpi = 10e-12
CM = Cmu * (1 + Av)
Cin = CM + Cpi
tau = Rs * Cin
fH = 1 / (2 * math.pi * tau)
Cout = Cmu * (1 + 1 / Av)
print(round(CM * 1e12, 2))
print(round(Cin * 1e12, 2))
print(round(fH / 1e3, 1))
print(round(Cout * 1e12, 2))

traps: Using |A_v| instead of (1 + |A_v|). At gain 4, C_M becomes 8 pF instead of 10 pF, a 20 % error.
Adding Cπ to Cμ and then multiplying the sum by gain. Only Cμ bridges input and output; Cπ goes to ground and is added once.
Using the signed gain. With A_v = −100, (1 − 100) = −99 gives negative capacitance. Use magnitude.
Multiplying output capacitance by full gain. Output sees Cμ(1 + 1/|A_v|) ≈ Cμ, not Cμ(1 + |A_v|).
Quoting fH as fT. fH is where this wired stage's gain falls to 0.707 of midband; fT is where transistor open-loop current gain reaches 1 — see Chapter 3.3.

quiz.a: Frequency where voltage gain magnitude falls to 1/√2 = 0.707 of midband, i.e. 3 dB below midband.

quiz.q: Name the two BJT hybrid-pi capacitances. Give a typical value and the junction each comes from.
quiz.a: Cπ, base to emitter, 10–200 pF, mostly diffusion capacitance of forward-biased emitter junction. Cμ, base to collector, 1–10 pF, mostly transition capacitance of reverse-biased collector-base junction.

quiz.q: A 2 pF capacitor connects output back to input of a stage with gain −100. Why does the input node behave as if 202 pF sat there?
quiz.a: Output moves 100 times as far as input, oppositely, so capacitor voltage is 101 times input voltage. It draws 101 times the current of a 2 pF capacitor to ground. A grounded capacitor with same current must be 101 times larger, i.e. 202 pF.

quiz.q: Why is CB free of Miller multiplication while CE is not?
quiz.a: In CB the base is grounded and input is emitter, so Cμ runs collector to ground and never bridges input and output. In CE, Cμ bridges base and collector, and collector swings by full gain, so current is multiplied by (1 + |A_v|).

quiz.q: A CE stage has |A_v| = 50, Cμ = 3 pF, Cπ = 12 pF, R_eq = 2 kΩ. Find C_M, total input capacitance and fH.
A CS stage has |A_v| = 20, Cgd = 2 pF, Cgs = 8 pF, R_eq = 5 kΩ. Find Miller capacitance at gate and fH.
A designer raises R_C to double CE midband gain. Explain two effects on fH.
quiz.a: First, Miller capacitance grows from Cμ(1 + A) to Cμ(1 + 2A), roughly doubling, so input time constant roughly doubles and input pole roughly halves. Second, output resistance R_C ‖ R_L rises, so output pole falls. Doubling gain costs roughly half the bandwidth.

quiz.q: In a cascode, a CB transistor sits above the input CE transistor. Why does this raise fH above plain CE?
quiz.a: The CB stage looks like about 1/gm, a few tens of ohms, at its emitter. The input transistor's collector moves by only about −1 times the base signal, so gain across its Cμ is near 1. Miller multiplication becomes about (1 + 1) = 2 instead of (1 + A). Input pole moves up by roughly A/2; output pole then limits the stage.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real design uses SPICE with full Gummel-Poon or BSIM models to find poles numerically. The Miller estimate still judges whether a stage will be fast. RF designers kill feedback capacitance with a cascode, neutralising capacitor, or common-base input. At microwave frequencies devices are described by S-parameters rather than voltage gain. Search for 'Miller capacitance', 'cascode frequency response' and 'unilateral gain'.
